documents: Garrett et al. 2022, Journal of Quaternary Science, published version (White Rose eprint PDF, 20 pages including repository cover)
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (page 1 is the White Rose repository cover; printed journal page = PDF page minus 1). Supplementary items are cited as S plus a number.

entry.evidence: establish whether the rapid rates of 20th century sea‐level rise can be replicated and accounted for using the latest microfossil‐based RSL reconstruction approaches

sequences.source_document: Garrett et al. 2022, J. Quaternary Sci., published version

steps.action: The abstract frames rival drivers of 20th century sea-level change (land-based ice melt versus regional sterodynamics) as hypotheses that the proxy records can test.
steps.quote: can test hypotheses about the drivers of 20th century global sea‐level change, including land‐based ice melt and regional sterodynamics

steps.action: The authors' earlier proxy reconstructions from Tasmania and Pounawea, which show a rapid early or mid-20th century rise, are cited as the starting result.
steps.quote: Existing proxy reconstructions from Tasmania and southern New Zealand provide evidence for a rapid early or mid‐20th century sea‐level rise

steps.action: Fadil et al. (2013) are cited for perceived discrepancies between the proxy rise and regional tide-gauge data, which challenge the earlier result.
steps.quote: in part due to perceived discrepancies with tide‐gauge data from the region

steps.action: The authors ask whether the rapid 20th century rates can be replicated at a new site (Mokomoko Inlet) and accounted for, and plan to improve the Pounawea record.
steps.quote: establish whether the rapid rates of 20th century sea‐level rise can be replicated and accounted for

steps.action: The authors collected 31 surface samples on a levelled transect at Mokomoko Inlet, Rose Bengal stained and counted foraminifera, and set a datum at the highest occurrence of foraminifera (about HAT).
steps.quote: we collected 31 surface samples along a 45‐m‐long transect from the upper tidal flat to the zone of terrestrial vegetation

steps.action: Before standardizing elevations to SWLI, the authors checked the TPXO8 tidal model against two tide gauges and a published tidal range.
steps.quote: The tidal model successfully replicates data from these tide gauges, with decimetre‐scale disparities

steps.action: The authors established elevation-dependent zonation of foraminifera at Mokomoko and in the combined regional dataset using PAM clustering, NMDS and DCCA (48.5% and 22.9% of variance explained by elevation).
steps.quote: Foraminifera show vertical zonation in the Mokomoko Inlet surface samples, as they do in the dataset from Pounawea

steps.action: The authors built local and regional WA, WAPLS and PLS transfer functions with bootstrapped cross-validation, removed one outlier from the regional set, lumped the Trochamminita species, and selected two-component WAPLS models.
steps.quote: We develop transfer functions based on both the local Mokomoko Inlet training set

steps.action: The authors tested a Bayesian transfer function as an alternative method (it performed worse and was rejected) and tested lumped versus split Trochamminita taxonomy (Supplement S3).
steps.quote: A Bayesian transfer function trained on the 53‐sample regional training set did not perform as well as the WAPLS model

steps.action: The authors logged the trench stratigraphy, took cores, and radiocarbon dated macrofossils; the radiocarbon dates show age reversals and modern ages from root contamination.
steps.quote: None of the contacts between successive fine‐grained sedimentary layers are abrupt or show evidence for erosion

steps.action: Because the radiocarbon results were problematic, the authors added chronohorizons (137Cs peak, Pb isotopes including the Tambora excursion, pine pollen) and built an rbacon age-depth model.
steps.quote: To address the issues encountered with the radiocarbon results, we applied other complementary dating approaches.

steps.action: The authors calibrated the fossil assemblages of core MKT-18.5 with the local and regional transfer functions to obtain palaeomarsh surface elevations with errors.
steps.quote: Calibration of the dead assemblages in core MKT‐18.5 using the local and regional transfer functions provides palaeomarsh surface elevation predictions

steps.action: The authors compared local and regional predictions (mean difference 0.01 m), assessed modern analogues with MinDC, and ran a joint NMDS of fossil and modern samples.
steps.quote: The predictions from the local and regional models are in strong agreement

steps.action: The reconstruction narrowly failed the randomTF significance test; the authors kept it and attributed the failure to low elevation variability in high-marsh sequences (Kemp et al. 2013).
steps.quote: Consequently, we do not view the significance test result as any cause for concern.

steps.action: The authors excluded low-count basal samples and core MKT-15.5 (suspected post-depositional modification), and assigned an HAT indicative meaning to the basal samples of MKT-5 and MKT-12.
steps.quote: Consequently, we do not use this core for reconstructing sea level.

steps.action: The authors corrected for GIA with a 5000-member ensemble and estimated GIA-corrected RSL and rates at Mokomoko with Gaussian process regression (peak 5.0 mm/a in 1940).
steps.quote: The rate of rise increased during the early 20th century

steps.action: The authors recalibrated the published Pounawea core with the regional transfer function and a new age-depth model, which gives a more finely resolved record.
steps.quote: we recalibrate the fossil foraminiferal assemblages reported by Gehrels et al. (2008) using the regional transfer function

steps.action: The authors compared the two independent marsh records and found a consistent rapid mid-20th century rise and a late-century slowdown.
steps.quote: The Pounawea and Mokomoko Inlet reconstructions provide a consistent picture of a rapid mid‐20th century sea‐level rise

steps.action: The authors compared the proxy records with the Dunedin tide gauge (since 1899) and found a smaller total rise and no clear mid-century acceleration in the instrumental record.
steps.quote: the Dunedin tide gauge records a smaller total rise and lacks clear evidence for more rapid rates

steps.action: The authors stated two rival explanations for the discrepancy: the proxies overestimate the rise, or the sites differ in RSL history (for example through vertical land motion).
steps.quote: This discrepancy could indicate that the tidal‐marsh records overestimate RSL rise or that the locations do not share a common RSL history

steps.action: The authors rejected the overestimation rivals (compaction, per Brain et al. 2012; a small training set) using the new regional training set and the agreement between the two sites.
steps.quote: we can also discount this possibility

steps.action: The authors weighed published cGPS, InSAR and seismic evidence on differential vertical land motion; the extrapolated short-term rates do not resolve the discrepancy, and earthquake deformation remains unknown.
steps.quote: Coseismic, postseismic and interseismic deformation remain largely unknown contributors to RSL changes in this region

steps.action: The authors kept the rapid 20th century rise as replicated, while stating that the tide-gauge discrepancy is not fully resolved.
steps.quote: replication of the rapid 20th century rates at a second tidal marsh provides additional weight to support the findings of Gehrels et al. (2008)

steps.action: The authors computed site sea-level budgets from barystatic (Frederikse et al. 2020), sterodynamic (SODAsi.3) and inverse-barometer components as the expectation of the stated drivers.
steps.quote: deriving a sea‐level budget for each location

steps.action: The authors compared the budgets with the GIA-corrected reconstructions; they match, including the 1940s peak, with the largest misfit in 1900-1920.
steps.quote: The budgets for Mokomoko Inlet and Pounawea show a high degree of similarity to our GIA‐corrected RSL reconstructions

steps.action: The authors judged enhanced Antarctic melt unlikely, because it would predict faster far-field Northern Hemisphere rises, which are not observed.
steps.quote: The rapid rates of sea‐level rise that we have reconstructed from New Zealand are unlikely to reflect enhanced Antarctic ice melt.

steps.action: The authors attributed the mid-20th century rapid rise chiefly to the sterodynamic component (linked to the IPO phase transition), with a barystatic contribution, and the late-century slowdown to the positive IPO phase.
steps.quote: it is the sterodynamic component that chiefly accounts for the particularly rapid rates of change in our budgets

No; inferred from fossil foraminifera through transfer functions and age models
Replicate the rapid rise at a second marsh and attribute its drivers
Proxy overestimation vs vertical land motion; barystatic vs sterodynamic vs Antarctic drivers
Partly: budget components differ in timing; Antarctic melt predicts faster Northern Hemisphere far-field rise

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes: two independent marshes record the same rise
Mostly: method and replication checks pass; significance test narrowly failed; tide-gauge mismatch remains
Sterodynamic processes are the best explanation for the mid-century rise

end.claim: The rapid mid-20th century sea-level rise along the coast of southern New Zealand was primarily driven by regional thermal expansion and ocean dynamics (sterodynamics), with a barystatic contribution.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the GIA-corrected proxy reconstructions with barystatic plus sterodynamic sea-level budgets, and finding they match including the 1940s peak, is what produces the attribution claim.

gates.evidence: The question of whether the earlier Pounawea rise replicates directed the choice of a second marsh, but the trench and cores date from December 2006 (p. 5), and the paper does not say what hypothesis guided their collection. The replication and the budget comparison could have failed. The significance test narrowly failed and was set aside (p. 13), and the tide-gauge mismatch remains unresolved (p. 15). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen; the selection thresholds (counts above 30 and 75, outliers beyond 2.5σ) follow published conventions.

imports.item: Gaussian process regression with Matern covariance (MATLAB fitgpr) and Monte Carlo ensemble
Bayesian age-depth modelling (rbacon, autoregressive gamma process)
Partitioning Around Medoids clustering with silhouette widths
NMDS with Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and DCCA constrained ordination (vegan, CANOCO)
Partial least squares regression (Wold et al. 1984), basis of PLS and WAPLS transfer functions
Multi-collector ICP-MS (Thermo Neptune) for lead isotope ratios
Low-background HPGe well-type gamma detector for 137Cs
Rose Bengal staining to separate living and dead foraminifera
Twentieth Century Reanalysis sea-level pressure for the inverse barometer effect

novelty_claims.quote: In this paper we present new proxy‐based sea‐level reconstructions for southern New Zealand spanning the last millennium.
we present a new late Holocene RSL record from Mokomoko Inlet, near Bluff, southern New Zealand
We develop a regional transfer function that provides crucial underpinning for enhanced sea‐level reconstructions from the Southern Hemisphere

limits: No peer-review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. The paper does not say when the questions were formed relative to fieldwork: the trench was logged in December 2006, many years before publication. The inference is that the replication framing may postdate data collection. The rival drivers are evaluated by agreement with budgets built from others' models, not by a crucial test that excludes a rival. Sub-claims at other statuses: the Mokomoko and Pounawea RSL and rate histories are estimate_with_resolution (peak 5.0 and 6.0 mm/a, with 95% intervals; p. 14). The regional WAPLS transfer function is capability_characterized (RMSEP 4.93 SWLI; p. 9). The replication of the rapid rise at a second marsh is kept as corroboration (p. 15). The discrepancy with the Dunedin tide gauge is left unresolved; vertical land motion is offered only as a feasible explanation (no_conclusion for that sub-question). The 95% interval for the 1940 peak rate is given differently in the Discussion (3.4–9.5) and the Conclusions (3.4–9.8). Both reconstructions narrowly fail the randomTF significance test; the authors dismiss this by citing prior work rather than testing it. Antarctic contributions are assumed constant, following Frederikse et al. (2020).

disagreements.target: Fadil et al. (2013): Pounawea sequence influenced by sediment compaction, overestimating RSL
disagreements.support: Cited compaction modelling (Brain et al. 2012) for thin marsh sequences on lithified rock, plus close agreement between two independent sites.
disagreements.quote: Fadil et al. (2013) suggest the Pounawea sequence could be influenced by sediment compaction, resulting in over‐ estimation of RSL.

disagreements.target: King et al. (2021): small modern training set of Gehrels et al. (2008) may bias accuracy
disagreements.support: A new, larger regional training set with good analogues gives a reconstruction consistent with the earlier one.
disagreements.quote: With the addition of new modern samples from Mokomoko Inlet and the development of a robust regional transfer function, we can also discount this possibility.

disagreements.target: Gehrels et al. (2008): exclusion of the Dunedin tide gauge for suspected wharf subsidence (Hannah, 2004)
disagreements.support: Following Denys et al. (2020), who confirmed the gauge's stability, the authors include Dunedin in the comparison.
disagreements.quote: While Gehrels et al. (2008) excluded the Dunedin record from their comparison due to suspected wharf subsidence (Hannah, 2004), Denys et al. (2020) subsequently confirmed [...]

disagreements.target: Southall et al. (2006) local Pounawea transfer function
disagreements.support: When low-count samples are removed, the Pounawea-only model has little predictive power; expressed relative to the sampled gradient, the new models perform better.
disagreements.quote: both of our transfer functions outperform the earlier model (~8% for the models presented here, 20% for the Pounawea model)

disagreements.target: Global attribution of the rapid 1930s-1940s rise to barystatic melt from glaciers and the Greenland Ice Sheet
disagreements.support: In the site budgets the sterodynamic component, not the barystatic one, chiefly produces the rapid local rates.
disagreements.quote: it is the sterodynamic component that chiefly accounts for the particularly rapid rates of change in our budgets
